technical.clientSecretHandling: Web App and Automated App clients are confidential: send Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret) to the token, refresh and revoke endpoints, plus code_verifier. Native and Single page apps are public: send client_id in the body and never ship a secret.

refreshTokens.notes: Issued only when offline.access is requested. Rotation and refresh-token lifetime are not documented; always store the latest refresh_token returned.

technical.accessTokenLifetime: About 2 hours; read expires_in from the token response
redirectUriRules: Must exactly match a callback URL allowlisted in the Developer Console, including trailing slashes
https in production; for local development use http://127.0.0.1, not localhost
javascript, data, file, ftp and mailto schemes are disallowed

stage1.summary: App creation and the OAuth flow are self-serve, but there is no free tier: you must prepay credits before billed calls (including the token check and any post) will work.

stage2.summary: Every read and post costs credits, with a monthly Post read cap. The agreement limits self-serve to apps with a limited number of end users; beyond that, you must apply for Enterprise. No app review is documented.

stage1DoneWhen.text: GET https://api.x.com/2/users/me with the user's Bearer access token returns 200 with data.id and data.username, and the token response included a refresh_token (because offline.access was requested).

blockedBy.how: Without a positive credit balance or under an exhausted spending limit, every request is blocked.
Sets prices and the monthly read cap, can review your use and change your tier, and requires Enterprise once you outgrow self-serve.

profiles.bottomLine: Setup takes one sitting, but nothing works until you prepay credits: no free tier exists. Each post costs about $0.015 and reads are capped monthly, and the agreement pushes apps with many users to Enterprise.
topRisks: No free tier: calls fail until you buy credits, and again whenever the balance or spending limit runs out
Self-serve is limited to apps with a limited number of end users; past that, Enterprise is required with no documented threshold
The monthly read cap is about 3 million, and quote-posts, likes and follows are Enterprise-only

steps.title: Sign in to the Developer Console and accept the agreement
instructions: Go to https://console.x.com and sign in with the X account that will own the app.
Review and accept the Developer Agreement and Policy. Pay-per-use is meant for prototypes and apps with a limited number of end users; larger use needs Enterprise.
Complete the profile with basic information about how you plan to use the API.

steps.title: Create the app
instructions: From the Console dashboard click New App (or Create App).
Enter the app name, description and use case. Describe the read-and-post features honestly; X can review use later.
The Console generates keys immediately. Anything it shows you is shown once, so save it to a secret manager right away.

steps.title: Turn on OAuth 2.0 and register the callback URL
instructions: In the app's settings, open User authentication settings > Setup.
App permissions: choose Read and write so posting works. Changing this later forces users to re-authorize.
Type of App: Web App for a server that keeps a secret (confidential). Use Native App or Single page App only if you can't keep a secret (public, PKCE only).
Callback URI / Redirect URL: add your callback exactly as your app will send it, including any trailing slash. Up to 10. Use https in production and http://127.0.0.1:PORT (not localhost) locally.
Fill in Website URL if the form asks for it (not confirmed as required on an official page).
Save.

links.label: Developer apps: callback URLs and app types

steps.title: Copy the OAuth 2.0 Client ID and Client Secret
instructions: On the app's Keys and Tokens page, copy the Client ID and (for Web App) the Client Secret.
Store the secret server-side only. If you lose it, regenerate it; the old one stops working.

steps.title: Buy API credits and set a spending limit
instructions: In the Developer Console, save a credit or debit card and buy credits. There is no free tier; requests fail without a positive balance.
Your first purchase can earn $20 in promotional credits (rolling out; they expire after 3 months).
Set a maximum spend per billing cycle. Optionally turn on auto-recharge (amount plus threshold).
It isn't documented whether the OAuth flow or /2/users/me works at zero balance; plan on buying credits before the check below.

steps.title: Send yourself through the authorize URL with PKCE
instructions: Generate a random code_verifier and its S256 code_challenge (plain is also accepted but only use it for testing), plus a random state up to 500 characters.

Open https://x.com/i/oauth2/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_CALLBACK&scope=tweet.read%20tweet.write%20users.read%20offline.access&state=STATE&code_challenge=CHALLENGE&code_challenge_method=S256
Add media.write to the scope if you will upload images or video.
Sign in as an X user and approve. X redirects to your callback with code and state; check that state matches.

steps.title: Exchange the code within 30 seconds
instructions: Immediately POST to https://api.x.com/2/oauth2/token (form-encoded) with code, grant_type=authorization_code, redirect_uri (same as before) and code_verifier.
Web App: send Authorization: Basic base64(CLIENT_ID:CLIENT_SECRET) and leave client_id out of the body. Public clients: send client_id in the body.
Store access_token (valid about two hours) and refresh_token. Refresh with grant_type=refresh_token before it expires.
Always store whatever refresh_token the refresh response returns; whether X rotates refresh tokens isn't documented.

steps.title: Check the token works
instructions: GET https://api.x.com/2/users/me with Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN.
Expect 200 with data.id, data.name and data.username.
Optionally POST https://api.x.com/2/tweets with {"text": "..."} and expect 201 with data.id. Each post costs credits.

steps.title: Set spend controls before real users connect
instructions: Size auto-recharge for bursty traffic: it fires at most once every 5 minutes and never at zero or negative balance.
Set a per-cycle spending limit and balance alerts. At the limit, every request is blocked until the next cycle.

steps.title: Monitor credits and the monthly read cap
instructions: Poll GET https://api.x.com/2/usage/tweets for daily Post consumption, or watch per-app usage in the Console.
Track progress toward your Post read cap per billing cycle (about 3 million); the Console shows the exact figure.
Handle 429 (rate limit or usage-capped) and request failures caused by an exhausted balance.

steps.title: Follow the posting and automation rules
instructions: Posts must be user-initiated. No unsolicited @mentions; replies only when the user engaged first.
If the app runs an automated account, turn on the Automated label and name the operator in the bio.
AI-generated replies need X's prior approval through the Policy Support form.

steps.title: Decide whether you need Enterprise
instructions: The agreement limits self-serve to prototypes and apps with a limited number of end users (no number given). Past that, or past the read cap, apply for Enterprise.
Quote-posts, likes and follows via the API are Enterprise-only now.

blockers.cause: The code is only valid for 30 seconds

nuances.text: PKCE is used even by confidential Web App clients: send code_verifier at the token exchange alongside the Basic auth header. Docs examples use plain; prefer S256.
Authorize on x.com/i/oauth2/authorize, but token, revoke and API calls go to api.x.com.
Use http://127.0.0.1, not localhost, for local development callbacks.
Access tokens are short-lived (about 2 hours); offline.access adds a refresh token. Use expires_in from the response.
Post reads per cycle: about 3 million. Check the Console for your exact cap.
Changing app permissions (e.g. Read to Read and write) requires existing users to re-authorize, so set Read and write before inviting users.
The authorization-code page's example uses account.follows.* scopes that its own scope table doesn't list; use the table names.
Existing OAuth 1.0a users can be moved to OAuth 2.0 with token exchange, without re-authorizing; offline.access is included.
On Account Activity API v2, OAuth 1.0a permissions override OAuth 2.0 scopes when both exist.
Basic and Pro may have been deprecated after the Feb 2026 launch; check current plans in the Console.
